title: Man. Post. Cap. IV: Secunda ratio — hoc fac et vives
pass_a_gloss: Second, This can be illustrated and confirmed by the promise and threat of the legal covenant. Life was promised, do this and you will live. What life? that spiritual one placed in justice and holiness? nothing less: the law promised neither its beginning nor progress nor continuation, but demanded them. The promises of the legal covenant were conditional. The condition was perfect justice perpetually preserved. Under this condition life was promised. Therefore the promised life could not be situated in the presence of justice. But now the death which the law threatened was formally opposed not to the condition but to the promised life: therefore it did not consist in the absence or privation of justice.
pass_b_english: Second proof. The legal covenant's own promise and threat make the same point. Life was pledged under the formula "do this and you will live." Was that the spiritual life grounded in righteousness and holiness? Far from it. The law never promised the start, growth, or continuance of that life; it demanded them. Legal-covenant promises were conditional, and the condition was perfect righteousness kept without break. Life was promised only under that condition—so the thing promised cannot have been identical with righteousness itself already present. And the death the law threatened stood formally over against the promised life, not against the condition. Hence that death was not the absence or stripping-away of righteousness.
source_text: Secunda, Hoc potest illustrari & confirmari promissione & comminatione foederis legalis. Pollicebatur vitam, hoc fac & vives. Quam? spiritualem illam positam in justitia & sanctitate? nihil minus: eius nec initium, nec progressum, nec continuationem lex promittebat, sed exigebat. Promissiones foederis legalis erant conditionales. Conditio erat perfecta justitia perpetuo conservata. Sub hac conditione promittebatur vita. Quare vita promissa non potuit sita esse in praesentia justitiae. Iam autem mors, quam lex comminabatur, opposita erat formaliter non conditioni, sed vitae promissae: non consistebat igitur in absentia seu privatione justitiae.
